bib.title: Chapter 6. RAG and Agents (AI Engineering)
bib.venue: book chapter (O'Reilly, AI Engineering); author and year are not printed in the PDF text, taken from the ledger title and the repo notes' citation

question: How should context be constructed for a foundation model per query, through retrieval (RAG) or tool-using agents, and how are these systems built, evaluated and given memory?
contributions: Overview of RAG: architecture, term-based and embedding-based retrieval, hybrid search, chunking, reranking, query rewriting, contextual retrieval, multimodal and tabular RAG
Framework for agents: environment, tools (knowledge augmentation, capability extension, write actions), planning, reflection, tool selection, failure modes and evaluation
Memory systems: internal knowledge, short-term and long-term memory, memory management

results.claim: A model at 95% accuracy per step falls to 60% over 10 steps and 0.6% over 100 steps, which is why agents need stronger models.
results.setup: Illustrative arithmetic: 95% per-step accuracy, errors compound across steps; no model or benchmark.
results.quote:
If the model’s accuracy is 95% per step, over 10 steps, the accuracy will
drop to 60%, and over 100 steps, the accuracy will be only 0.6%.

results.claim: Chameleon (GPT-4 plus 13 tools) improves the best published few-shot result on ScienceQA by 11.37%.
results.setup: Chameleon (Lu et al., 2023), GPT-4-powered agent with 13 tools vs best published few-shot result on ScienceQA.
results.quote:
Chameleon improves
the best published few-shot result by 11.37%.

results.claim: Chameleon improves accuracy on TabMWP by 17%.
results.setup: Chameleon (Lu et al., 2023), GPT-4 agent with 13 tools on TabMWP (tabular math word problems); baseline not named in the chapter.
results.note: Chapter does not say whether the 17% is points or relative, or against which baseline.

results.claim: Anthropic advises that a knowledge base under 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages) can go whole into a Claude prompt without RAG.
results.setup: Guidance for Claude models; Anthropic (2024) as quoted by Huyen.
results.quote:
if “your knowledge base is smaller than
200,000 tokens (about 500 pages of material), you can just include the entire knowledge
base in the prompt that you give the model, with no need for RAG or similar methods”

results.claim: Vector database spend is often one-fifth to half of model API spend at some companies.
results.setup: Anecdotal; no sample, companies or period given.
results.quote:
It’s not uncommon to see a company’s vec-
tor database spending be one-fifth or even half of their spending on model APIs.

results.claim: RRF default constant k is typically 60.
results.setup: Reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack et al., 2009) combining ranked lists from several retrievers.
results.quote: A typical value for k is 60.

results.claim: Example chunking setting: 2,048-character chunks with 20 characters of overlap.
results.setup: Illustration only; the chapter says there is no universal best chunk or overlap size.
results.quote:
If you set the chunk size to be 2,048 characters, you can perhaps
set the overlapping size to be 20 characters.

results.claim: IVF is typically set so that each cluster holds on average 100 to 10,000 vectors.
results.setup: IVF (Sivic and Zisserman, 2003) with K-means clustering; rule of thumb, no benchmark.
results.quote:
it’s typical to set
the number of clusters so that, on average, there are 100 to 10,000 vectors
in each cluster.

results.claim: Anthropic's contextual retrieval prepends an LLM-generated context of usually 50-100 tokens to each chunk before indexing.
results.setup: Anthropic (2024) Contextual Retrieval; no retrieval-quality numbers given in the chapter.
results.quote:
Anthropic used AI models to gener-
ate a short context, usually 50-100 tokens, that explains the chunk and its relation-
ship to the original document.

results.claim: Tool inventories in the literature range from 5 tools (Toolformer) to 13 (Chameleon) to 1,645 APIs (Gorilla).
results.source: Schick et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2023; Patil et al., 2023
results.setup: Toolformer finetuned GPT-J; Chameleon GPT-4; Gorilla prompted to select among APIs.
results.quote:
Toolformer (Schick et
al., 2023) finetuned GPT-J to learn five tools. Chameleon (Lu et al., 2023) uses 13
tools. On the other hand, Gorilla (Patil et al., 2023) attempted to prompt agents to
select the right API call among 1,645 APIs.

results.claim: BEIR supports retrieval systems across 14 common retrieval benchmarks.
results.quote:
BEIR (Benchmarking IR) (Thakur et al., 2021) is an evaluation har-
ness for retrieval. It supports retrieval systems across 14 common retrieval
benchmarks.

results.claim: Term-based retrieval is much faster and cheaper than embedding-based; embedding-based can outperform it after finetuning.
Planning should be decoupled from execution so only validated plans run; reflection is easy to implement and can bring surprisingly good gains at the cost of latency and tokens.

limits: The agents section is flagged by the author as experimental: no established theoretical frameworks for defining, developing and evaluating agents.
Almost no measurements of its own: numbers are reported from Chameleon and Anthropic, are worked examples, or are anecdotes.
Whether LLMs can plan is left open; the author notes evidence is anecdotal.
Tools, APIs and frameworks named (Elasticsearch, FAISS, AutoGPT, Composio, function-calling APIs) date to 2024-25.
Pseudocode for function calling is representative of multiple APIs, not a specific one.
practices: Evaluate a RAG system both component by component and end to end: retrieval quality, final output, and embeddings (Comparing retrieval algorithms).
Measure context precision and context recall; recall needs every document labelled per query, so many frameworks support only precision (Comparing retrieval algorithms).
Use rank-aware metrics (NDCG, MAP, MRR) when ordering matters (Comparing retrieval algorithms).
Combine retrievers in production: sequence (cheap term-based, then precise rerank) or parallel with reciprocal rank fusion (Combining retrieval algorithms).
Use BM25 or Elasticsearch as a strong, cheap baseline before embedding-based retrieval (Comparing retrieval algorithms; Summary).
Add keywords or entities (e.g. error codes) as metadata so embedded chunks stay findable by exact term (Contextual retrieval).
Experiment to find chunk size and overlap; there is no universal best (Chunking strategy).
Keep chunk size within the generator's and embedder's context limits; token-based chunking requires reindexing if the tokenizer changes (Chunking strategy).
Rewrite ambiguous conversational queries before retrieval; if identity cannot be resolved, say so rather than hallucinate (Query rewriting).
Rerank by time for time-sensitive data; order still matters in context reranking because models attend better to the start and end (Reranking).
For tabular data, use text-to-SQL, execute, then generate; add a table-selection step when schemas do not fit in context (RAG with tabular data).
Decouple planning from execution and validate plans with heuristics or AI judges before running them (Planning overview).
Add an intent classifier, including an IRRELEVANT class, to reject out-of-scope requests (Planning overview).
Keep humans in the loop for risky write actions and define the level of automation per action (Planning overview; Write actions).
Always have the system report the parameter values of each function call and inspect them (Function calling tip).
Prefer natural-language plans over exact function names so plans survive tool API changes, with a translator to commands (Planning granularity).
Plan hierarchically to resolve the plan-detail trade-off (Planning granularity).
Check which control flows (sequential, parallel, if, for loop) an agent framework supports (Complex plans).
Choose tools by comparing tool sets, ablating tools, and inspecting tool-call distributions and tool transitions (Tool selection).

Evaluate agents on planning failures (invalid tool, invalid parameters, wrong values, goal failure, reflection errors), tool failures and efficiency (steps, cost, latency) (Agent Failure Modes and Evaluation).
Test each tool independently and print every tool call and output (Tool failures).
Put essential-for-all-tasks information in the model via training, rarely needed information in long-term memory, immediate information in short-term context (Memory).
Manage short-term memory with FIFO, summarisation, or reflection-based insert/merge/replace; FIFO can lose the opening purpose of a chat (Memory).

terms.definition: a technique that enhances a model’s generation by retrieving the relevant information from external memory sources
retrieval by keyword/lexical match, scored by TF-IDF or BM25 using an inverted index; the book prefers this over 'sparse'
semantic retrieval: rank documents by how closely their embedding aligns with the query embedding, using a vector database
combining term-based retrieval and embedding-based retrieval
combines rankings from several retrievers by summing per-ranking scores of the form 1/(k+rank), with k typically 60
Out of all the documents retrieved, what percentage is relevant to the query?
Out of all the documents that are relevant to the query, what percentage is retrieved?
anything that can perceive its environment and act upon that environment
the set of tools an agent has access to
read-only actions let an agent perceive the environment; write actions let it act upon and change it
the order in which actions can be executed: sequential, parallel, if statement, for loop
the model's context; fast to access but limited, and does not persist across tasks
external data sources accessed via retrieval, persisted across tasks and deletable without updating the model
knowledge the model retains from its training data; unchanged unless the model is updated
